intended:
PR description: This change introduces a connection pool for the Redis client. Previously every request opened a new connection and closed it afterwards, which was fine at low traffic, but under load we saw connection churn and occasional timeouts. The pool is configured with a maximum of 20 connections and a minimum of 5 idle, and the numbers come from the config so they can be tuned per environment. I also added a health check that pings the pool on startup so we fail fast if Redis is unreachable.

Testing: I ran the load test script before and after, and the p95 dropped from 110 milliseconds to about 40. I also added unit tests for the config parsing.

Please look closely at the shutdown path because I want to be sure we close the pool cleanly.

spoken: this module implements the leader election, uh it works by having every node try to create the same key in etcd with a ttl, whoever succeeds is the leader and keeps refreshing the lease, if the leader dies the key expires and another node takes over, note that there can be a short window of up to one ttl where there are zero leaders but never two, as long as clocks dont drift more than the ttl, so the work done by the leader must tolerate being interrupted
intended: This module implements the leader election. It works by having every node try to create the same key in etcd with a TTL. Whoever succeeds is the leader and keeps refreshing the lease. If the leader dies, the key expires and another node takes over. Note that there can be a short window of up to one TTL where there are zero leaders, but never two, as long as clocks don't drift more than the TTL. So the work done by the leader must tolerate being interrupted.

spoken: ok so this is my review of the schema change, first the good, adding the tenant id column with a not null constraint and a foreign key is the right call, and i like that you did the backfill in a separate migration, second the concern, the backfill updates all rows in a single transaction, and the events table has about eighty million rows, so it will hold locks for a long time and probably blow up the replication lag, i would batch it, ten thousand rows at a time with a short sleep between batches, third, the index is created without the concurrently keyword, on a table that size that blocks writes, so please use create index concurrently, and note that it cant run inside a transaction so it needs its own migration, with those two changes i think this is good to go
intended: Okay, this is my review of the schema change. First, the good: adding the tenant_id column with a NOT NULL constraint and a foreign key is the right call, and I like that you did the backfill in a separate migration. Second, the concern: the backfill updates all rows in a single transaction, and the events table has about 80 million rows, so it will hold locks for a long time and probably blow up the replication lag. I would batch it, 10,000 rows at a time with a short sleep between batches. Third, the index is created without the CONCURRENTLY keyword. On a table that size, that blocks writes, so please use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, and note that it can't run inside a transaction, so it needs its own migration. With those two changes, I think this is good to go.

spoken: alright so kestrel has a problem with its job scheduler, um let me explain what i think is happening, jobs are stored in a table with a status column and a run at timestamp, and the scheduler polls every second, selects the due jobs and marks them running, but it does the select and the update in two separate queries without a lock, so if we run two scheduler instances, which we do in production, both can pick up the same job, i saw a job run twice last night and i think thats why, so i want you to change it to a single query that claims the jobs atomically, in postgres that would be update with a subquery using for update skip locked and returning the rows, limit the batch to fifty, and make sure the claim also sets a heartbeat timestamp so a reaper can find jobs whose worker died, then add a test that starts two schedulers against the same table with a hundred jobs and asserts that each job ran exactly once
intended: Alright, so Kestrel has a problem with its job scheduler. Let me explain what I think is happening. Jobs are stored in a table with a status column and a run_at timestamp, and the scheduler polls every second, selects the due jobs, and marks them running. But it does the select and the update in two separate queries without a lock, so if we run two scheduler instances, which we do in production, both can pick up the same job. In Postgres, that would be an UPDATE with a subquery using FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and RETURNING the rows. Limit the batch to 50, and make sure the claim also sets a heartbeat timestamp so a reaper can find jobs whose worker died. Then add a test that starts two schedulers against the same table with 100 jobs and asserts that each job ran exactly once.

spoken: so i did a deeper analysis of the performance regression and heres what i found, um first the regression started with the release on the fourth, not the one on the sixth like we thought, because the dashboard i was looking at averages over a week and hid it, second the cause is the new permissions check, which loads the full role tree from the database on every request instead of caching it per user, it adds about thirty milliseconds, third it only shows up on endpoints that call the check more than once, like the project list, which calls it for every row, so the fix is to cache the role tree per request and to batch the check for lists, i have a branch with the first part and it brings the p ninety five back to where it was, the batching is a bigger change so id split it into a separate pr, let me know if you agree
intended: I did a deeper analysis of the performance regression, and here's what I found. First, the regression started with the release on the 4th, not the one on the 6th like we thought, because the dashboard I was looking at averages over a week and hid it. Second, the cause is the new permissions check, which loads the full role tree from the database on every request instead of caching it per user. It adds about 30 milliseconds. Third, it only shows up on endpoints that call the check more than once, like the project list, which calls it for every row. So the fix is to cache the role tree per request and to batch the check for lists. I have a branch with the first part, and it brings the p95 back to where it was. The batching is a bigger change, so I'd split it into a separate PR. Let me know if you agree.

PR description

Summary: Upgrades the Postgres driver from version 4 to version 5.

Why: Version 4 is end of life, and the new version fixes the connection leak we saw in the incident last month.

What changed: The pool configuration options were renamed, so I updated the config loader and the docs. The transaction API now returns a context object instead of a client, so the repository layer changed in about 30 places, mostly mechanical.

How I tested it: The full test suite passes, I ran the load test for an hour and the connection count stayed flat, and I tested a rollback of the deploy.

Risks: The new driver is stricter about parameter types, so a couple of queries that passed strings for integers now fail. I fixed the ones I found, but there might be others, so watch the error logs after the deploy.

intended:
Subject: Proposal to adopt trunk-based development

Hi all,

I'd like to propose that we move from long-lived feature branches to trunk-based development.

The main problem today is that branches live for a week or more, so merges are painful and reviews are huge. In trunk-based development, we merge small changes to main at least daily, hide unfinished work behind feature flags, and rely on the CI pipeline to keep main always releasable.

The prerequisites are a fast and reliable test suite, which we are close to, and a flag system, which we already have.

If you're interested, I'll set up a pilot with the platform team for one month and report back.

Thanks

spoken: pull request for harbor, title, add tag immutability rules, um so this adds a way to mark tags as immutable by a regex pattern per repository, for example release dash star, once a tag matches a rule you cant overwrite it or delete it through the api, only an admin can remove the rule first, the motivation is that someone re pushed a release tag last month and broke a deploy, the implementation adds a rules table, a check in the push and delete handlers, and a small admin endpoint to manage rules, i also added an audit log entry whenever a push is rejected, what to look at, the regex matching is anchored at both ends, which i think is the safe default, but id like a second opinion, whats not included, the ui for managing rules, that comes in a follow up, tests cover the happy path, rejected overwrite, rejected delete and the admin override
intended:
Pull request for Harbor

Title: Add tag immutability rules

This adds a way to mark tags as immutable by a regex pattern per repository, for example release-*. Once a tag matches a rule, you can't overwrite it or delete it through the API. Only an admin can remove the rule first. The motivation is that someone re-pushed a release tag last month and broke a deploy. The implementation adds a rules table, a check in the push and delete handlers, and a small admin endpoint to manage rules. I also added an audit log entry whenever a push is rejected.

What to look at: the regex matching is anchored at both ends, which I think is the safe default, but I'd like a second opinion.

What's not included: the UI for managing rules. That comes in a follow-up.

Tests cover the happy path, rejected overwrite, rejected delete, and the admin override.

spoken: architecture decision record, title, use event sourcing for the ledger, status, accepted, context, the ledger must be fully auditable and we need to answer what was the balance at any past point in time, a mutable balance column cant do that without extra history tables, decision, we store every change as an immutable event and derive balances by replaying them, with periodic snapshots for speed, consequences, reads are more complex and need projections, the team needs to learn the pattern, and schema changes to events need careful versioning, but we get a complete audit trail and easy time travel queries
intended:
Architecture decision record

Title: Use event sourcing for the ledger

Status: Accepted

Context: The ledger must be fully auditable, and we need to answer "what was the balance at any past point in time?" A mutable balance column can't do that without extra history tables.

Decision: We store every change as an immutable event and derive balances by replaying them, with periodic snapshots for speed.

Consequences: Reads are more complex and need projections, the team needs to learn the pattern, and schema changes to events need careful versioning. But we get a complete audit trail and easy time-travel queries.

spoken: code review for the saffron search feature, overall the structure is good and i like the separation between the query builder and the executor, um a few things though, first the query builder concatenates the search term into the sql string, i know you escape quotes but please use bound parameters, escaping is how injections happen, second the results are not paginated, if someone searches for a single letter we return the whole table, add a limit and an offset or a cursor, third the debounce on the frontend is zero milliseconds which defeats the purpose, three hundred is the usual number, fourth the empty state says no results found even while the request is loading, so users see a flash of the wrong message, show a spinner until the response arrives, and last a question, why did you choose to lowercase on the client instead of using a case insensitive collation in the database, i think the collation is cleaner, but i could be missing a reason
intended: Code review for the Saffron search feature. Overall the structure is good, and I like the separation between the query builder and the executor. A few things though. First, the query builder concatenates the search term into the SQL string. I know you escape quotes, but please use bound parameters. Escaping is how injections happen. Second, the results are not paginated. If someone searches for a single letter, we return the whole table. Add a limit and an offset or a cursor. Third, the debounce on the frontend is 0 milliseconds, which defeats the purpose. 300 is the usual number. Fourth, the empty state says "No results found" even while the request is loading, so users see a flash of the wrong message. Show a spinner until the response arrives. And last, a question: why did you choose to lowercase on the client instead of using a case-insensitive collation in the database? I think the collation is cleaner, but I could be missing a reason.

spoken: module overview, this is the lumen rendering pipeline, a frame goes through four stages, culling, where we drop everything outside the camera, sorting, where we order draw calls by material to reduce state changes, batching, where we merge compatible meshes, and submission, where we record the command buffer, each stage only reads the output of the previous one and never touches shared state, which is what makes it safe to run culling and sorting for the next frame while the gpu is still busy with the current one, if you add a stage keep that property, or you will introduce a race that only shows up under load
intended: Module overview: this is the Lumen rendering pipeline. A frame goes through four stages. Culling, where we drop everything outside the camera. Sorting, where we order draw calls by material to reduce state changes. Batching, where we merge compatible meshes. And submission, where we record the command buffer. Each stage only reads the output of the previous one and never touches shared state, which is what makes it safe to run culling and sorting for the next frame while the GPU is still busy with the current one. If you add a stage, keep that property, or you will introduce a race that only shows up under load.
